title: Choosing up and down from volatility
objectives: Calibrate the tree’s up and down moves to a volatility.
Explain why $\ln u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$ matches the share’s variance per step.

screens.title: Spread from volatility
screens.prose: A share costs £100. We split one year into four quarterly steps. The slider sets the share’s volatility $\sigma$, a yearly measure of how much it swings. The tree turns $\sigma$ into each quarter’s $u$ and $d$.
screens.question: Move $\sigma$. What happens to the middle price after four quarters?

options.why: Watch the middle leaf as you move the slider. Two ups and two downs cancel exactly.
Watch the middle leaf as you move the slider. Two ups and two downs cancel exactly.

options.text: It moves, but less than the outer prices
options.why: The outer prices move, but the middle leaf holds still at £100 for every $\sigma$.

hints.text: Set $\sigma$ to 10%, then to 40%, and read the middle leaf each time.
The middle leaf has two ups and two downs.

feedback.correct: Two ups and two downs bring the share back to £100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the middle leaf at two very different values of $\sigma$.

explain.text: Two ups and two downs bring the share back to £100, whatever $\sigma$ is. So $d = 1/u$: a down move undoes an up move. A higher $\sigma$ only spreads the outer prices.

state.caption: $\sigma = 20\%$: each quarter the price is multiplied by $u$ or by $d$

hints.text: A down move must undo an up move.
Up then down must give back £100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the $d$ that makes $u \times d = 1$.

byKey.mirror: You took $2 - u$, a 10.52% fall to mirror the rise. Then $ud = 0.9889$, and the middle price drifts below £100.
byKey.half-sigma: You took $1 - \sigma/2$. Then $ud = 0.9947$, so up then down would not return to £100.
byKey.level1: 0.8 belongs to level 1’s one-year tree. A quarter must move less.

explain.text: $d = 1/u = 0.9048$, so $ud = 1$ and the tree recombines around £100. A fall of 9.52% undoes a rise of 10.52%.

screens.title: How the step scales
screens.prose: Here is $\ln u$ for the same share with three step lengths. A step four times shorter does not move four times less.
screens.question: What is $\ln u$ for a step of 1/16 of a year?

widget.label: $\ln u$ for 1/16 of a year
widget.accept: 0.05: each step four times shorter halves $\ln u$.

hints.text: Going from 1 year to ¼ of a year divides $\ln u$ by how much?
A step 4 times shorter halves $\ln u$.
1/16 is 4 times shorter than ¼, so halve 0.1 again.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what happened to $\ln u$ when the step went from 1 year to ¼.

byKey.linear: You divided 0.2 by 16, as if the move shrank with the step length. Dividing $\Delta t$ by 4 only halved $\ln u$.
byKey.same: That is the quarter’s value. A step of 1/16 is shorter still, so it moves less.
byKey.quarter: You divided 0.1 by 4. The table shows a 4 times shorter step halves $\ln u$.

explain.text: Each time $\Delta t$ shrinks 4 times, $\ln u$ halves, so it scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$. This is the **Cox-Ross-Rubinstein** choice: $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$ and $d = 1/u$. For 1/16 of a year, $u = e^{0.05} = 1.0513$.

screens.title: The weight per step
screens.prose: Over one step, £1 grows to $e^{r\Delta t}$ with continuous compounding. So level 1’s $q$ becomes $$q = \dfrac{e^{r\Delta t} - d}{u - d}.$$ Take $r = 5\%$, $\Delta t = 0.25$, $u = 1.1052$ and $d = 0.9048$.
screens.question: What is $q$, to 4 decimal places?

hints.text: First find $e^{r\Delta t}$ for one quarter.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow £1 for one quarter, not a year, then use the formula.

byKey.annual: You grew £1 for a whole year, $e^{0.05}$. One step is a quarter: $e^{0.05 \times 0.25}$.
byKey.annual-simple: You used $1 + r = 1.05$, a whole year’s growth. One step is a quarter: $e^{0.0125}$.
byKey.half: Equal weights ignore interest. The share must grow at the risk-free rate on average, so $q$ is a little above ½.

explain.text: $e^{0.0125} = 1.0126$, so $q = (1.0126 - 0.9048)/(1.1052 - 0.9048) = 0.5378$. It sits just above ½ because the share must grow at the risk-free rate under $q$. As $\Delta t$ shrinks, $q$ moves towards ½.

screens.title: Level 1’s factors, every quarter
screens.prose: A colleague builds the quarterly tree with $u = 1 + \sigma = 1.2$ and $d = 0.8$, the numbers from level 1. Her top price after a year is $100 \times 1.2^4 = $ £207.36.
screens.question: What is wrong with her tree?

options.text: Each quarter swings as much as a whole year should, so the year is far too wide
Nothing: $1 + \sigma$ is the up move for any step
options.why: You kept $u = 1.2$ for a quarter. A shorter step must move less: $\ln u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t} = 0.1$.

canvas.caption: Her tree: each quarter as wide as a year

options.text: Only $d$ is wrong: it should be $1/1.2$
options.why: Fixing $d$ keeps each quarter as wide as a year. The up move itself must shrink with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$.

canvas.caption: With $d = 1/1.2$: still each quarter as wide as a year

options.why: You scaled the move with $\Delta t$. Variance grows with time, so the move scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$: 0.1, not 0.05.

canvas.caption: Moves scaled with $\Delta t$: far too narrow

hints.text: How wide should one quarter be, compared with a whole year?
The table showed a step 4 times shorter halves $\ln u$.
For a quarter, $\ln u = 0.2 \times \sqrt{0.25} = 0.1$, so $u = 1.1052$ and the top price is £149.18.

feedback.correct: Her quarters are each a year wide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare one quarter’s move with one year’s.

byKey.nothing: You kept $u = 1.2$ for a quarter. A shorter step must move less: $\ln u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t} = 0.1$.
byKey.linear: You scaled the move with $\Delta t$. Variance grows with time, so the move scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$: 0.1, not 0.05.

explain.text: Her tree treats each quarter as a year, so four steps spread like four years: $1.2^4 = 2.07$. With $u = e^{0.2 \times 0.5} = 1.1052$ the top is £149.18. The move per step must shrink with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$.

screens.title: Why the square root
screens.prose: Let $X = \ln(S_{\text{next}}/S)$ be one step’s log-return, with weight $q$ on up. Since $d = 1/u$, $X$ is $+\ln u$ or $-\ln u$. We want $\mathrm{Var}(X) = \sigma^2\Delta t$, the share’s variance over one step.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $E[X] = q\ln u - (1-q)\ln u = (2q - 1)\ln u$: weight the two outcomes
$E[X^2] = (\ln u)^2$: both outcomes square to the same number
Set $(\ln u)^2 = \sigma^2\Delta t$, so $\ln u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$

hints.text: The variance needs $E[X]$ and $E[X^2]$ first.
The small-$\Delta t$ approximation is used just before matching $\sigma^2\Delta t$.
Mean and mean square, then the variance, then let $\Delta t$ shrink, then match.

feedback.correct: Moments, variance, the small-step limit, then the match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the variance from the two moments before approximating.

byKey.e: Matching to $\sigma^2\Delta t$ needs the variance in terms of $\ln u$ first, so it comes last.
byKey.c: The variance formula uses both $E[X]$ and $E[X^2]$, so those come first.

explain.text: With our numbers $4q(1-q) = 4(0.5378)(0.4622) = 0.994$, so the variance is within 1% of $\sigma^2\Delta t = 0.01$. Over $n$ independent steps the variances add to $\sigma^2 T$. That is why $\ln u$ scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$, not with $\Delta t$.

screens.title: No volatility at all
screens.prose: Set $\sigma = 0$. Then $u = d = 1$, and $q = \dfrac{e^{r\Delta t} - 1}{0}$: the formula breaks. A share that cannot move is riskless, so without arbitrage it must grow at the rate $r = 5\%$.
screens.question: What is a one-year call struck at £100 on this share worth today?

widget.label: Call value, in £
widget.accept: £4.88: the share ends at $100e^{0.05} = 105.13$, so the call pays £5.13 for sure; $5.13e^{-0.05} = 4.88$.

hints.text: Where must a riskless share be in a year?
It grows like money in the bank: $100e^{0.05} = 105.13$.
The call pays $105.13 - 100 = 5.13$ for sure. Discount it by $e^{-0.05}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow the share at the risk-free rate, take the sure payoff, then discount.

byKey.flat: You used the flat tree, where the share stays at £100. A riskless share must grow at 5%, to £105.13.
byKey.no-disc: £5.13 is paid in a year. Discount it by $e^{-0.05}$.
byKey.annual: You used $100/1.05$, annual compounding. This lesson compounds continuously: $100e^{-0.05}$.

explain.text: The share ends at $100e^{0.05} = 105.13$ for sure, so the call pays £5.13 for sure. Discounted, that is $S_0 - Ke^{-rT} = $ £4.88. With no volatility an option is worth only its discounted sure payoff.

screens.title: Four quarters to expiry
screens.prose: Back to $\sigma = 20\%$. A leaf with $j$ ups and $4 - j$ downs is $100u^jd^{4-j}$, which is $100e^{0.1(2j - 4)}$. A call struck at £100 expires there.
screens.question: Fill in the top two leaves and the call’s payoff there.

hints.text: Four ups add four lots of $\ln u = 0.1$.
Three ups and one down leave a net of two ups.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $100e^{0.1(2j - 4)}$ for each leaf, then subtract the strike.

byKey.r1c1: Three ups and a down: the down cancels one up, so $100e^{0.2} = 122.14$.
byKey.r0c2: The payoff is the share price minus £100.
byKey.r1c2: The payoff is the share price minus £100.

explain.text: Only the top two leaves pay: £49.18 and £22.14. The leaves are spaced evenly in log price, 0.2 apart. That even spacing is what $d = 1/u$ buys.

screens.title: Quoting a one-year call
screens.prose: A client asks for a one-year call on this £100 share, struck at £100. Volatility is 20% and $r = 5\%$. Price it on the four-step tree.
screens.question: What is the call worth today?

hints.text: Weight each payoff, add, then discount for one year.
Only the top two rows pay.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add weight times payoff over the rows, then discount by $e^{-0.05}$.

byKey.no-disc: You weighted correctly but did not discount. Four quarterly discounts make $e^{-0.05}$.
byKey.no-paths: You left out the 4 paths to three ups. Use the weight column, which includes them.
byKey.half: You used $q = \tfrac{1}{2}$. The risk-neutral weight here is 0.5378.

explain.text: $e^{-0.05}(0.0837 \times 49.18 + 0.2876 \times 22.14) = $ £9.97. The Black-Scholes formula gives £10.45 for the same inputs. Four steps leave the tree 48p short; level 3 shows the gap closing as the steps shrink.

ideas: Choose $d = 1/u$, so up then down returns to the start and the tree recombines.
A step of length $\Delta t$ moves by $\ln u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$, so its log-return variance is about $\sigma^2\Delta t$.
Use the rate for one step too: $q = \dfrac{e^{r\Delta t} - d}{u - d}$.

formula.name: Cox-Ross-Rubinstein tree
formula.tex: u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}, \quad d = \dfrac{1}{u}, \quad q = \dfrac{e^{r\Delta t} - d}{u - d}
formula.note: Needs $d < e^{r\Delta t} < u$; very small $\sigma$ or long steps can break it.

summary.trap: $u = 1 + \sigma$ makes every step as wide as a year. Scale the move with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$.

quiz.prose: A share has volatility 30%. You build a tree with monthly steps.
quiz.question: What is $u$, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$ with $\Delta t = 1/12$.

byKey.one-plus: That is $1 + \sigma$, a whole year’s move. A month must move less.
byKey.linear: You used $\sigma\Delta t$ in the exponent. The move scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$.
byKey.linear-simple: You used $1 + \sigma/12$. The move scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$, not $\Delta t$.

quiz.prose: You halve the length of every step in a CRR tree and keep $\sigma$ fixed.
quiz.question: What happens to $\ln u$?

options.why: Halving would make the variance per year fall. $\ln u$ scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$, so it is multiplied by $\sqrt{1/2}$.
Then the tree would get wider with more steps. Shorter steps must move less.
Shorter steps move less, not more.

explain.text: $\ln u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$, so halving $\Delta t$ multiplies it by $\sqrt{1/2} \approx 0.71$. Twice as many steps, each with half the variance, keep the year’s variance at $\sigma^2$.

quiz.prose: A one-step CRR tree covers a whole year: $\sigma = 20\%$, $r = 5\%$, so $u = 1.2214$ and $d = 0.8187$.
quiz.question: What is $q$, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $q = (e^{r\Delta t} - d)/(u - d)$ with $\Delta t = 1$.

byKey.simple: You used $1.05$. This tree compounds continuously: $e^{0.05} = 1.0513$.
byKey.half: Equal weights ignore interest. $q$ must make the share grow at the risk-free rate.

explain.text: $q = (e^{0.05} - 0.8187)/(1.2214 - 0.8187) = 0.5775$. With one long step, $q$ sits further from ½ than with quarterly steps (0.5378).

quiz.prose: A CRR tree has quarterly steps, $r = 5\%$ and $\sigma = 1\%$. Then $u = e^{0.005} = 1.0050$, while one quarter’s growth is $e^{0.0125} = 1.0126$.
quiz.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: $q$ comes out above 1: the best step loses to the bank, so the tree allows arbitrage
Nothing: $q$ is just close to ½
options.why: Compute it: $(1.0126 - 0.9950)/(1.0050 - 0.9950) = 1.76$. A weight above 1 is not a probability.
The top, $1.0126 - 0.9950$, is positive. It is larger than $u - d$, so $q > 1$.

options.text: The tree collapses to one price
options.why: The tree still has $u \ne d$. The problem is that $e^{r\Delta t} > u$.

feedback.correct: $q = 1.76$: the condition $d < e^{r\Delta t} < u$ fails.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $q$ and compare $e^{r\Delta t}$ with $u$.

explain.text: Here $e^{r\Delta t} = 1.0126 > u = 1.0050$, so level 1’s no-arbitrage condition fails and $q = 1.76$. CRR needs $\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t} > r\Delta t$. Shorter steps fix it, since $\sqrt{\Delta t}$ shrinks more slowly than $\Delta t$.
